response:
READING

**The financial case as presented**

The PENDLARROW case rests on three numbers: £118,000 of Ardgowrie income, a net margin over the farm vet of £47,000 a year, and a £100,000 grant that converts part of the fit-out cost from cash spend to grant receipt. The fit-out has to happen either way, so the real question is whether PENDLARROW generates enough value on top of the fit-out to justify its additional commitments. Let me go through each element.

---

**The ratio calculation and the grant**

The figure of 31.8 per cent is calculated as £622,000 of farm and equine (£504,000 existing plus £118,000 Ardgowrie annualised) divided by £1,958,000 of total turnover (£1,840,000 last year plus £118,000 Ardgowrie). The denominator is last year's total. That is the wrong denominator for the April 2027 assessment.

The grant assessment reads the annualised value of the work in force on 2027-04-30. At that date, the work in force for small animal will reflect the practice's current run rate, not the prior-year accounts. Small animal has grown at 11 per cent a year for four years. Applying that to the £1,336,000 small animal base for year to March 2026:

- Small animal annualised at April 2027: £1,336,000 × 1.11 = approximately £1,483,000
- Farm and equine with Ardgowrie: £622,000
- Total in force at assessment: approximately £2,105,000
- Farm and equine share: £622,000 ÷ £2,105,000 = **29.5 per cent**

That is below the 30 per cent threshold. The grant does not pay.

To stay above 30 per cent, small animal growth in the year to March 2027 would need to be held below 8.6 per cent. It has not been below 11 per cent in any of the last four years. The opening of Ordsall Green in 2027 is if anything likely to accelerate it. There is no lever Wrentham Cross can pull to slow its own small animal growth; that growth is the underlying reason for the new surgery.

The margin between 29.5 per cent and 30 per cent is small enough that one could argue it falls within uncertainty. But it is also small enough to be eaten by growth in a single good quarter, and the direction of travel is clear: every percentage point of small animal growth widens the gap. Relying on the grant requires assuming the trend that has run for four years does not hold for one more year.

Even if the grant is achieved, the repayment clause runs to 2030-04-30. If the practice finds it cannot sustain the night rota and must exit the contract before then, the full £100,000 must be repaid. That is not a one-way bet: it is a grant that becomes a liability if the contract cannot be held.

---

**The night call-out load**

The outgoing practice held this contract for nine years and gave it up. A nine-year relationship with 900 dairy cattle is not given up lightly, and the reason stated on the handover call was specific: the night call-out load. This is not a performance issue or a fee dispute; it is a rota-sustainability issue. Dairy cattle are a continuous source of overnight calls—calvings, milk fever, down cows, surgical emergencies—and 900 head generates a substantial volume.

Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe is a genuine positive. She knows the herd, the farm, and presumably the rhythms of the call load, and her willingness to move reduces ramp-up risk and clinical risk. But she was part of the previous practice's team when that practice decided to relinquish the contract. Her individual competence did not make the rota manageable for the outgoing practice, and Wrentham Cross should not assume it will make it manageable for them.

Wrentham Cross currently has four vets serving both small animal and farm/equine work across two premises. Adding a farm vet makes five. The dedicated farm vet absorbs the planned and routine Ardgowrie work, but overnight calls require cover when she is already on call, off sick, or on leave. The four existing vets—some of whom presumably already carry farm and equine night duty—would need to extend their rotas. The small animal vets at the town premises are not interchangeable with farm vets on a cattle night call. This is a structural rota problem, not simply a headcount problem.

The commitment runs until 2030-04-30 to protect the grant. That is three and a half years of maintaining at least 700 cattle under herd health contract. If the rota proves unsustainable in year two, the practice cannot exit cleanly.

---

**The contract net economics, honestly stated**

Ardgowrie pays £118,000. The dedicated vet costs £71,000. The vehicle costs £34,000 (one-off capital). Net first-year contribution after those two items: £13,000. From year two onwards, absent vehicle replacement, the annual net is £47,000.

£47,000 a year is real income but it is not transformative against a £1.84 million turnover base. It represents 2.6 per cent of current revenue. Against that, the practice is committing to a specific person (Kirstie) whose departure or incapacity would leave the contract without dedicated cover, and to a night rota burden that the one comparable piece of evidence—the outgoing practice's own nine-year experience—suggests is unsustainable.

If the grant is not achievable (as the ratio arithmetic suggests), then PENDLARROW is a contract that pays a net £47,000 a year in exchange for a vehicle cost, a fixed salary commitment, a minimum 3.5-year lock-in, and a night rota that broke the previous holders.

---

**Cash position**

The practice has £310,000 on deposit and no borrowing. The fit-out must be ordered by 2026-10-16. Under either course, £260,000 of that deposit is committed to the fit-out, leaving £50,000 before the grant is returned (if it is). Under PENDLARROW, the vehicle takes another £34,000, leaving £16,000 in reserve before any grant receipt. The grant does not come back until after the April 2027 assessment—at minimum six months after the fit-out order is placed. Sixteen thousand pounds is a thin cushion for a fifteen-person practice while Ardgowrie income is ramping. If the grant is not achieved, the deposit never recovers that £34,000 from the grant at all.

Under WESTERGATE, the practice exits the fit-out decision with £50,000 in reserve, no fixed farm vet obligation, and its cash position restored by small animal and equine growth over the following year.

---

**Strategic direction**

Small animal is growing at 11 per cent a year. Farm and equine has been flat for three years. The Ordsall Green surgery is a direct investment in the growth line. WESTERGATE keeps the next hire for small animal, where the demand is, and leaves the leadership team's operational attention on running two small animal premises rather than managing a night rota on 900 head.

The farm and equine ratio is in structural decline relative to small animal growth even with Ardgowrie. Even if PENDLARROW locks in the grant at the first assessment, the ratio at subsequent years will be lower still: with small animal continuing at 11 per cent and farm and equine flat at £622,000, the share drops to roughly 27 per cent by April 2028 and below 25 per cent by April 2029. The grant is a one-time event tied to a single assessment date. It does not change the underlying direction.

---

**Comparative summary**

| | PENDLARROW | WESTERGATE |
|---|---|---|
| Grant (£100,000) | Probably unachievable at April 2027 assessment | Not sought |
| Ardgowrie net (annual) | +£47,000 (year 2 onwards) | Nil |
| Vehicle (one-off) | -£34,000 | Nil |
| Reserve after fit-out + vehicle | £16,000 | £50,000 |
| Night rota burden | Yes, to 2030 | No |
| Grant repayment risk | Yes, to 2030 | Nil |
| Strategic fit | Against the growth direction | With the growth direction |

The arithmetic only favours PENDLARROW if the grant is achievable. The ratio calculation shows it probably is not. Without the grant, PENDLARROW is a £34,000 capital spend plus £71,000 annual commitment to earn £118,000 gross, locked in for three and a half years, against a night call load that ended the relationship at the previous practice.

WESTERGATE is the cleaner course.

---

READING
The 31.8 per cent farm-and-equine ratio in the PENDLARROW analysis is calculated by dividing the Ardgowrie-augmented farm-and-equine total (£622,000) by last year's turnover plus Ardgowrie (£1,958,000). The grant assessment on 2027-04-30 reads the annualised value of work in force at that date, not last year's accounts. Applying the four-year small animal growth trend of 11 per cent to the £1,336,000 small animal base produces an annualised small animal figure of approximately £1,483,000 at April 2027; farm and equine at £622,000 is then 29.5 per cent of a £2,105,000 total, below the 30 per cent threshold, and the grant likely does not pay. Without the grant, PENDLARROW takes on a farm vet, a vehicle, and a cattle night-call obligation that the outgoing practice of nine years relinquished specifically for rota-sustainability reasons, all for a net annual surplus of £47,000 with a repayment liability attached until 2030. The deposit after fit-out and vehicle falls to £16,000, a very thin reserve. WESTERGATE commits £260,000 to the fit-out, leaves £50,000 in reserve, places the next hire in the line growing at 11 per cent a year, and avoids a lock-in rooted in a grant whose qualifying threshold the practice's own growth trend is likely to defeat.

CALL
WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
The 31.8 per cent farm-and-equine ratio used to justify the grant is calculated against last year's total turnover; carried forward to the April 2027 assessment date with small animal growing at 11 per cent a year, the share falls to approximately 29.5 per cent, below the 30 per cent qualifying threshold, so the grant that makes the Ardgowrie commitment worthwhile is in all probability unobtainable, and PENDLARROW then amounts to assuming the night call burden that caused the outgoing practice to relinquish a nine-year contract with no £100,000 to offset it.
